name: Context and system landscape
what: A wide-angle map of the people, services, boundaries, and external systems that make a product work.
when: Use it when someone needs orientation before component details, or when ownership and system boundaries are unclear.
example: OpenClaw from message arrival to channel delivery, with the Gateway, agent runtime, models, skills, MCP servers, and durable state in one frame.

name: Progressive architecture zoom
what: Several views of one system that reveal detail gradually while preserving names and spatial anchors.
when: Use it when one diagram would either overwhelm a newcomer or hide the runtime mechanics an experienced engineer needs.
example: An OpenClaw recurring report shown as a journey, then as subsystem responsibilities, then as one isolated agent turn announced to Telegram.

name: Request and interaction sequence
what: A time-ordered trace showing who calls whom, what crosses each boundary, and where the response returns.
when: Use it for debugging a request, explaining control flow, or locating the exact handoff where latency or behavior changes.
example: A Telegram message moving through the OpenClaw channel adapter, Gateway, session, agent runtime, model, tools, and outbound delivery.

name: State lifecycle
what: A map of valid states, transition triggers, terminal outcomes, and the loops that return work to a safe state.
when: Use it when behavior depends more on lifecycle than component layout—jobs, sessions, approvals, retries, or connection state.
example: An OpenClaw scheduled job moving through scheduled, queued, running, retrying, completed, and failed states.

name: Data transformation pipeline
what: A pipeline that emphasizes how information changes shape, meaning, validation status, and destination.
when: Use it when the important question is what happens to data rather than which function executes next.
example: An inbound OpenClaw webhook transformed from raw HTTP into a normalized event, model context, assistant output, and channel payload.

name: Dependency and deployment topology
what: A structural graph of runtime dependencies, deployment boundaries, shared resources, and external integrations.
when: Use it for blast-radius analysis, deployment planning, dependency ownership, or understanding what must be present at runtime.
example: The OpenClaw Gateway connected to plugins, model providers, local state, MCP servers, channels, and optional nodes.

name: Layered responsibility stack
what: A stack of conceptual layers that separates user intent, orchestration, execution, capabilities, and infrastructure.
when: Use it to explain responsibility boundaries, API depth, or why a change belongs at one layer instead of another.
example: OpenClaw arranged from Control UI and channels down through Gateway orchestration, agent execution, skills and tools, then providers and state.

name: Event timeline and history
what: A chronological story that aligns events, state changes, and observable evidence across participants.
when: Use it for incidents, automation runs, migrations, or any question where ordering and elapsed time explain the outcome.
example: One OpenClaw automation tick from scheduler wake-up through isolated session creation, report generation, persistence, and Telegram announcement.

name: Failure and recovery paths
what: A happy path paired with failure branches, detection signals, retry policy, fallback behavior, and final operator visibility.
when: Use it when reliability matters and a normal-flow diagram would conceal the system’s real operational behavior.
example: An OpenClaw report automation recovering from model, persistence, and Telegram delivery failures without duplicating completed work.

name: Decision and tradeoff matrix
what: A criteria-led comparison that makes tradeoffs visible and ends with a decision rule rather than a universal winner.
when: Use it when several architectures or tools are plausible and the choice depends on isolation, context, delivery, or operational cost.
example: Choosing among OpenClaw main-session system events, isolated agent turns, and webhooks for an automation.
